subject: Vocabulary
topic: Government / governance themed words — mixed tiers
description: Words about governance, power, rule, authority, state institutions — exam-frequent

options.option_text: Government by the people
Government by a small group of individuals (often a wealthy or powerful elite)
Government by one person
Absence of government

questions.explanation: Oligarchy — Greek 'oligos' (few) + 'arkhē' (rule); rule by few, often via wealth/family/military. Examples: post-Soviet Russian oligarchs; ancient Sparta. Related -ARCHY words (rule of/by): MONARCHY (one ruler — kings/queens); ANARCHY (no ruler — chaos or stateless society); HIERARCHY (rule by sacred / ranked order); MATRIARCHY (rule by mothers / women); PATRIARCHY (rule by fathers / men); PLUTOCRACY (rule by the wealthy — Greek 'ploutos' wealth). Same suffix family: -CRACY (Greek 'kratos' = power).

options.option_text: A senior judicial officer
A direct vote by the entire electorate on a single specific issue (e.g., independence, constitutional change)
A type of legislative committee
A foreign-policy treaty

questions.explanation: Plebiscite (also called REFERENDUM) — Latin 'plebs' (commoners) + 'scitum' (decree). A nationwide public vote on a single question. Historic examples: 1947 Sylhet plebiscite (joining Pakistan or Assam); Brexit referendum (2016, UK); 2014 Scottish independence vote; 1969 Sikkim → India merger; 2017 Catalonia independence (deemed illegal by Spain). Plebiscite vs Referendum — broadly interchangeable, though referendum implies a constitutionally-mandated vote and plebiscite a specific consultative one. India does NOT have a national plebiscite mechanism; some Latin American + European democracies use them frequently.

options.option_text: A democratically elected leader
A ruler who holds absolute power, unchecked by constitution or elections
A junior bureaucrat
An economist

questions.explanation: Autocrat — Greek 'autos' (self) + 'kratos' (power) → 'self-ruler'. A leader with absolute, unchecked power. Related: AUTOCRACY (the system); DICTATORSHIP (often used interchangeably; Latin origin). Other related: TYRANT (Greek; an unjust ruler — modern meaning of cruel oppressor); DESPOT (Greek; absolute ruler); AUTHORITARIAN (concentrated authority, but allows some pluralism); TOTALITARIAN (state controls all aspects of public + private life — Hannah Arendt's analysis of Nazi/Soviet regimes). DEMAGOGUE — a populist leader who exploits emotions to gain power (Trump, Putin, Modi-critics use this label politically).

questions.topic: Government / governance themed words — mixed tiers

options.option_text: Is governed by a king
Has supreme, independent authority within its territory, free from external control
Is run by religious clergy
Has a monarch as head

questions.explanation: Sovereign — Latin 'super' (above). A state with full independent authority (internally + externally). The Preamble of the Indian Constitution begins: 'We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN socialist secular democratic republic'. Related: SOVEREIGNTY (the quality); 'Westphalian sovereignty' — modern state-system principle from the 1648 Peace of Westphalia. Compare REPUBLIC (a state where power lies with the people via elected representatives, not a hereditary monarch); MONARCHY (a hereditary head of state); FEDERATION (power shared between central + state governments). India is a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic.

options.option_text: Bribery of officials
Manipulating electoral district boundaries to favour a particular political party
Voting twice in the same election
Banning a candidate from contesting

questions.explanation: Gerrymandering — coined 1812 from US Massachusetts Governor Elbridge GERRY + 'salamander' (the salamander-shaped district map he approved). Means redrawing electoral district lines to benefit one party — by 'packing' opposition voters into few districts (waste their majority votes) or 'cracking' them across many (dilute below-majority everywhere). India's Delimitation Commission (constitutional body, Article 82) draws Lok Sabha + Assembly constituencies to prevent partisan distortion — its decisions cannot be challenged in court. The current delimitation is based on the 2001 Census; next will be after the first census post-2026 (recently constitutionally amended to allow this).

options.option_text: Foreign diplomat
Independent official appointed to investigate complaints against public administrators / institutions
Senior court judge
Member of an electoral commission

questions.explanation: Ombudsman — Swedish for 'representative'; Sweden first instituted the office (1809). An independent commissioner who investigates complaints of maladministration / corruption against public officials. India's institutions in this lineage: LOKPAL (national, set up 2019 under the Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act 2013; jurisdiction includes the PM, with safeguards); LOKAYUKTA (state-level; first set up in Maharashtra 1971; Karnataka, Kerala, MP have had high-profile cases); RBI Banking Ombudsman (now Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021). Origin of the demand for Lokpal in India — 1966 Administrative Reforms Commission, M.C. Setalvad recommendation; Anna Hazare's 2011 'India Against Corruption' movement gave it final political momentum.

options.option_text: The military is in power
Religious leaders / religious law govern, with the state ruled in the name of a god / divine authority
Scientists make laws
Industrialists control policy

questions.explanation: Theocracy — Greek 'theos' (god) + 'kratos' (rule). Modern examples: Iran (Islamic Republic; Ayatollah/Guardian Council have ultimate authority); Vatican City (Pope is head of state). Saudi Arabia is sometimes labelled theocratic but is constitutionally an absolute monarchy (with Sharia as basic law). Israel is a JEWISH STATE but not a theocracy (it's a parliamentary democracy). India — SECULAR (Preamble, post 42nd Amendment 1976); the state has no religion + treats all religions equally. Other governance terms — STRATOCRACY (military rule), MERITOCRACY (rule by the talented), KAKISTOCRACY (rule by the worst), KLEPTOCRACY (rule by thieves), GERONTOCRACY (rule by the old).

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the meaning of 'suffrage' in a political context?

options.option_text: the authority to hold public office without facing an election
the right to cast a vote in public or political elections
the power to challenge and veto a legislative bill in parliament
the privilege of addressing the legislature on national policy

questions.explanation: Suffrage means the legal right to vote in elections. Option A describes eligibility to stand for office (candidacy), which is distinct from suffrage. Option C describes the veto power, held by an executive, not a voter.

questions.stem: In political vocabulary, which of the following best defines 'incumbent'?

options.option_text: a person who currently holds an elected or appointed public office
a candidate who is contesting an election for the very first time
an official temporarily assigned to fill an unexpected legislative seat
a politician who recently withdrew from a scheduled election contest

questions.explanation: Incumbent refers to the current holder of a position or office. Option B describes a political debutant or 'challenger', not an incumbent. Incumbents are already in office and often enjoy an advantage called the 'incumbency advantage'.

questions.stem: A legislature described as 'bicameral' is one that:

options.option_text: is jointly governed by two political parties forming a coalition
consists of two separate and distinct law-making chambers or houses
holds two separate sittings of parliament within each calendar year
allows both elected representatives and nominated experts to vote equally

questions.explanation: Bicameral comes from Latin 'bi' (two) + 'camera' (chamber). India's Parliament is bicameral — Lok Sabha (lower) and Rajya Sabha (upper). Option A confuses it with coalition government, a different concept entirely unrelated to the structural division of chambers.

questions.stem: The term 'quorum' in the context of a parliamentary or official proceeding refers to:

options.option_text: the certified verbatim record of all debates kept by the secretariat
the special majority required to pass a constitutional amendment clause
the minimum number of members whose presence makes proceedings valid
the fixed interval of days within which a fresh session must be convened

questions.explanation: Quorum is the minimum attendance needed for a body to legally transact business. Under Article 100 of the Indian Constitution, quorum for each House is one-tenth of total membership. Option B describes 'special majority', a separate requirement applicable only to constitutional amendments.

questions.stem: In the context of international law and diplomacy, 'ratification' of a treaty means:

options.option_text: the preliminary signing of a treaty by authorised state representatives
the renegotiation of key treaty terms between the signatory governments
the unilateral withdrawal of a member state from a previously signed accord
the formal confirmation by a state authority that makes a treaty binding

questions.explanation: Ratification is the official approval step — by parliament, the head of state, or a constitutional body — that converts a signed treaty into a legally binding obligation. Option A (signing) is the earlier step; signing indicates intent, while ratification creates binding legal force.

questions.stem: When a head of state orders the 'prorogation' of parliament, the specific legal effect is that:

options.option_text: the current parliamentary session ends but the parliament itself remains intact
parliament is permanently dissolved and fresh general elections must follow
all pending legislative powers transfer to a constituted emergency committee
a minister is formally removed following a successful no-confidence resolution

questions.explanation: Prorogation terminates only the current session; the parliament survives and pending bills lapse but can be re-introduced. Option B describes dissolution (under Article 85 in India), which ends the Lok Sabha's term and triggers elections — a far more drastic step with different constitutional consequences.

questions.stem: In legislative parlance, a 'filibuster' is most precisely described as:

options.option_text: a procedural vote invoked to immediately terminate debate and force a decision
a formal petition disputing the constitutional validity of a proposed bill
deliberate use of prolonged debate or speech to delay or prevent legislation
introducing several unrelated bills simultaneously so as to stall the schedule

questions.explanation: A filibuster is an obstructive tactic — a member speaks at extraordinary length to exhaust debate time and block a vote. It is especially associated with the US Senate. Option A is actually the opposite — that procedure is called 'cloture' (or 'closure' in Westminster systems), the mechanism used to end a filibuster.
